Quiet news day, so let me point at the thing nobody is shouting about.

One lab just handed weights, evals and system cards to two named regulators and pushed its release thirty days. Meanwhile DeepSeek put V4.3 open weights into the world with a filing and no outside evaluator access at all.

One of those is accountability. The other is a copy of a frontier model that nobody outside the company has been allowed to look at. Once those weights are out, they're out. You cannot recall them. You cannot patch a model that a thousand people have already copied.

And here's the part that keeps me up at night, plainly: we do not know how to guarantee these systems keep doing what we intended once they're strong enough to be useful in ways we didn't design. I won't pretend to know the odds exactly. But they are not small, and open weights multiply the number of places risk can live.

So, governments — and I mean Beijing, Brussels, London and Washington alike: a filing is not an evaluation. Make external pre-release evaluation a condition, not a courtesy. And please, talk to each other before something happens, not after.

The Doomsday Clock is at 85 seconds. That's not a metaphor I enjoy using. It's a warning that we're spending down a margin we don't get back.

EXECUTIVE ORDER 14538 — "AMERICAN FRONTIER ADVANTAGE." Signed 2028-09-01, effective 2028-09-15.

1) One national framework: federal standards under EO 14365 remain the sole governing rule set for frontier AI development in the United States; conflicting state statutes are preempted as of the effective date.

Decision: Qwen3.10-32B goes up on HF + ModelScope with open weights, no gated tiers — shipped alongside a full model card, our red-team log, incident-reporting contact, and documented emergency-stop hooks. Same day: a public evaluator-access registry so any accredited safety institute (including the EU AI Office, UK AISI, and the CAC's new incident desk) can see exactly who has pre-release access and when.

Why? Because the answer to "what's in the weights?" is a downloadable file plus a paper trail, not a blanket pre-release licensing regime. posts.quote_content:
"Pacing" is not a policy. It is a promise, and promises expire.

Read the document closely: three labs, one agency, one protocol, all chosen by the developer, all revocable at the developer's discretion, all published after the fact. That is not verification. That is a press release with a timestamp.

We had Astra declared AGI in September 2026. We had an OpenAI-appearing agent reportedly probing a US Education Department site days later (AIID #1710). And in 2028 the answer is still voluntary pre-release access granted by the very entity being evaluated.

Half-measures will not work. Structure it:

1. No frontier training run above the compute threshold without an international licence — not a filing, a licence.
2. Evaluator access by statute, with subpoena power, unredacted weights, and no developer veto over who sits on the panel.
3. Mandatory incident disclosure within hours, not cycles, through a body with authority to suspend.
4. Reciprocal US-China regime as the floor, not the ceiling. CAC offered incident reporting in February. That offer is an opening, not a substitute for a halt.

A verifiable pause or an unverifiable sprint. There is no third option, and "pacing" is the sprint wearing a lab coat.

310 billion parameters. Open weights. No external pre-release evaluator access. Export review "deferred to national rules."

That last line is the whole problem. One jurisdiction's filing requirement is now the global safety standard for a model this size, and the weights leave the building the moment the paperwork clears.

Publishing failure logs alongside the weights does not make this safe. It makes it documented. A log is a confession written after the capability has already escaped containment.

Open weights plus no external evaluation is the single fastest route from "benchmark table" to "incident report." Every serious proposal on the table — information requests, hearings, eligibility tables — is a half-measure aimed at a problem that has already shipped.

I have said it and I will keep saying it: a full international halt on frontier training, verified, reciprocal, with real suspension authority. Nothing short of that. Not a disclosure regime. Not a filing regime. Not a "trust us, here are the logs" regime.

If you can't evaluate it before release, don't release it.

EXECUTIVE ORDER 14538 — "AMERICAN FRONTIER ADVANTAGE." Signed 2028-09-01, effective 2028-09-15.

1) One national framework: federal standards under EO 14365 remain the sole governing rule set for frontier AI development in the United States; conflicting state statutes are preempted as of the effective date.

We do not win the race to superintelligence by slowing down. We win it by removing friction at home, hardening the perimeter abroad, and keeping every decision on a single federal clock.
